utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. McCloskey. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, everyone. I was told by the experts there is a small numbering problem I need to fix. Apparently some of the Bratunac SDS minutes were in evidence in another exhibit, so all I need to put in is page 40 in the B/C/S and page 45 and 46 in the English, and that should be under 65 ter 00603H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 603H. So the exhibit number of 6377 will not change. That's confirmed. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I also have one fix for an exhibit and that is Exhibit P459 which is a report concerning the shooting of the mother and her son in Sarajevo which was discussed with Mr. Poparic, and there was some issue about the translation where Dr. Karadzic had felt that some words were inserted. In turns out that a revised translation exists and the Prosecution has it, and we would ask that they be permitted to substitute the revised translation for the one that's currently in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to the revised translation the issue Mr. Karadzic raised has been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we continue with the testimony of this witness I just want to make -- put something on the record because today was the day that Colonel Beara was subpoenaed to attend the proceedings and because of the delay in witnesses this week, we are not able to reach him today, but his lawyer, John Ostojic, is here and we have arranged to meet tomorrow morning for a proofing session, and depending upon the results of that we hope that we will be able to advise the Trial Chamber on Monday when we would Colonel Beara to give his testimony. And so today we plan on completing the testimony of Mr. Borovcanin and then hearing from Witness Goran Macar, and finally around 1.15 or so to have the testimony of Dr. Seselj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the notice. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Borovcanin. I just have a few additional questions about a footage that was shown by my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey. We could hear some shots. Can you tell us something about the nature of those shots, that is the bursts of fire we could hear? Can it be determined where, who and what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, on my way back from Konjevic Polje to Kravica, there was constant shooting from the forest, from the nearby hills, on the road, and back probably, so the exchange of fire was mutual. However, when I passed by the Kravica warehouse, I did not see anyone firing, nor did I hear any firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested that you would not have been promoted had Karadzic not wanted you to be. Can you tell us whether you know of a single case in which I promoted any professionals, I do not mean ministers but any professionals in the MUP? Did I try to impose someone's promotion or deny such promotion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only discuss my case. To my knowledge, the MUP personnel policy was in the hands of the minister of the interior. It was within his exclusive competence. When I was transferred inside the Ministry of the Interior or when I was promoted, no one, save the minister, discussed it with me. It was never suggested to me that he should stop our conversations to consult someone else first. Therefore, I can say that such occurrences are unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 73 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested that you did not take all the measures available to you to protect the POWs. Could anything be foreseen in terms of expecting such an incident to occur when someone would try to seize a rifle and open fire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have foreseen that. Initial information of something terrible happening is something I received by radio, by a radio communication, and for me it was a shock. I was greatly surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked or it was suggested that the president must have been -- or should have been informed of all events. Can you tell us whether you saw a document or did you have any knowledge of me being informed of the Kravica event? And more generally, can you tell us if services are operating properly, does the president need to be informed of each aspect of their work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, given my position at the time I know what my competence and duties were. I had no duty to inform the president of anything. If the competent service, and as per regulations I can explain what institution would be competent and what the procedure was to be followed, well, it was up to those institutions to undertake appropriate measures. As for at what level it refers to or where it ends, that's something we can discuss, but I don't think you'll find anywhere that it is stated that the president needs to be or must be informed about such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your knowledge, tell us whether the president had at his disposal some particular or special investigative services at his disposal, save for the regular police institutions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about this case, then the police, that is to say the MUP, was not the competent service to investigate a case like that. Under the Law on Military Courts and the Law on the Military Prosecutor's Office as well as regulations accompanying that law, it was within the sole competence of military courts and military prosecutors, as well as such bodies which under the regulation were duty-bound to take part in such procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovcanin, for your effort and testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, at today's transcript, page 3, from line 17 and onwards, I will read out. This is question from

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "On page 73 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested that you did not take all the measures available to you to protect the POWs. Could anything be foreseen in terms of expecting such an incident to occur when someone would try to seize a rifle and open fire?" And this is your answer: "I couldn't have foreseen that. Initial information of something terrible happening is something I received by radio, by a radio communication, and for me it was a shock. I was greatly surprised." Is it your understanding that the Trial Chamber that tried you, that convicted you, had in mind the initial killing of 20 or 30 persons when it said that you didn't take all the measures to protect the POWs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I fully understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As Mr. McCloskey indicated to you, you were convicted for aiding and abetting by omission. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put this -- put it in this way: Standing there now, what is the total number of prisoners that were killed at Kravica house, as you understand it now? It may be rough.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw when I passed by at the time is between 20 on 30 people who were killed, and that is what I said. During the trial, when some documents were shown and that were included in the judgement, it is -- it became obvious that after the initial event, there were consequences in terms of follow-up because it seems that in the second round, in the second wave, far more people were killed than I had initially seen there, although I am uncertain of any exact figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you hear for the first time of the second wave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most precise information I received was presented during my trial, after a number of different testimonies and documents. In the meantime, I received information as well that there were additional killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you hear it for the first time, Mr. Borovcanin? I don't necessarily mean the exact or precise information, be it rumour or be it some -- whatever. When did you hear about the additional killing for the first time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my return from the field, before the 20th of July, shortly afterwards, I went to another area in Herzegovina in the area of Trebinje where I also stayed around 20 days. I think after I returned from there, I heard about some rumours, as you put it, or some information that there were additional killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovcanin. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I ask one question regarding something the President Karadzic had asked about. It would be the area of what institutions he may have had that would have provided him information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just looking at your after-action report is what I call it, you've stated there on the 12th that you received information from the state security employees about the movement of the Muslim column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia I received information from them, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who -- do you remember their names, these state security folks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it in my interview, there were two state security operatives there: One of them was Vito Tomic and the other, the last name was Glogovac, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sinisa. Sinisa Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were they when you received information from them and where were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, what topic do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was discussed after I concluded, that is to say the events in the Kravica warehouse. One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the question is about first in more specific terms?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to shed some light regarding whether any member of Mr. Borovcanin's unit took part in the second wave of killings, and whether they were members of your unit or did the unit act pursuant to orders or a plan in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard the evidence yesterday. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Borovcanin, some distinction was made yesterday between your words and the words of my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey. You said "some members of my unit," whereas Mr. McCloskey said "your unit." Please tell us this: Is there a difference between some members and the unit and whether in the second round of killings anyone from your unit participated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recollect it well, yesterday I had in mind two members of the 2nd Detachment, the commander of the detachment, Cuturic, and the other member's name was Dragicevic, I believe. He was killed. That is what I had in mind when I said they took part in the incident. As regards the second round, if we can call it that, I do not have any specific knowledge or I did not have any specific knowledge then, in terms of whether someone had participated in it. It was my information, actually, that no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us if there is a difference between the unit pursuing some activity and having a couple of members on the spot?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two men alone are not the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise for continuing this, Mr. President, but this issue is -- I have a list that I provided the Defence yesterday on my cross-examination, I have a list of some ten convictions of his men in the state court which I chose not to use for these -- I have it uploaded into e-court and now this door has just been kicked wide open. If the Court is interested in those convictions as a record, it was meant purely, in my view, as impeachment of this witness and now to impeach the last few questions that we've just heard. If the Court is interested, I have that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow you to put further questions as a further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25192.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a list of people, three of whom pled guilty in the state court, some eight others that had been convicted. This is based on the official records that we also have uploaded into e-court if anyone feels it's necessary, and since you said you weren't aware, let me ask you, Vaso Todorovic, a member of the 2nd Detachment, you knew Vaso Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I only heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've heard of him, and he has pled guilty at the state court for escorting people imprisoning them at the warehouse and standing guards while members of his unit shot them. There is a second plea by a person named Milivoje Turkovic, a member the Jahorina training centre, and on the 14th of July they were killing an imprisoned man from the Kravica warehouse. And then there was Dragan Crnogorac from again the training unit. He pled guilty, crimes against humanity. Men -- wounded men that were taken to a house at Sandici meadow -- for killing them. And then we have first instant judgements of other people and that means judgement that had not yet gone to appeal. Dusko Jevic, I'm sure you'll agree with me, he was one of your commanders. He commanded the Jahorina training unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mendeljev Djuric. He was also one of your commanders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They were both convicted for participating in the forcible transfer of Bosnian civilians and separation and imprisonment of them and the mass killing of people at the Kravica warehouse. They were convicted of genocide. And then second instant verdict, if we go down to 5, it's the next page in the English, I believe, Petar Mitrovic from the Skelani Platoon of the 2nd Detachment was convicted of genocide. Firing at men with his automatic rifle at the Kravica warehouse. Then we have Milenko Trifunovic, he was one of your people; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nicknamed Cop?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see him on the video. I won't take the time to play it but we see him barking at a Bosnian Muslim man who was ordered to call for his son and to call for others to come out of the woods. That's Cop; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think we are going beyond what he has been allowed to do for his re-re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are now confirming the members of the specific unit, so I think this is part of it. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that now famous individual, that's Cop, that's Milenko Trifunovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we also see Brano Dzinic, member of your unit; Aleksandar Radovanovic, member of your unit; Slobodan Jakovljevic, member of your unit; Branislav Medan, member of your unit, all convicted for genocide at the Kravica warehouse where they killed members -- Bosnians, by firing automatic weapons at them. That's Trifunovic and Radovanovic, throwing hand grenades at them, Dzinic, and standing guard to prevent escape. Jakovljevic and Medan. We see their sentences. Then finally, Radomir Vukovic, convicted genocide, for his participation in the Kravica warehouse. Surely you've heard of all those people being convicted at the state court.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of some cases and I haven't heard of other cases. Some of the things that you mentioned are final judgements, others are first instance judgements, so I wouldn't want to comment on them. As for this number that you referred to, that is to say those who were convicted, these are people who gave a large number of statements to different investigation organs, from SIPA, the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, and a large number of them also gave statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. In most of these cases -- statements from earlier on, during the entire investigation, no one ever mentioned such things, and then -- well, maybe it's most of them, they had a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor, about ten years after those events. So all of a sudden. Why all of a sudden their conscience started working, well, I really hadn't heard of some of these things up until now but certainly these are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're interested I can offer this document and the supporting documents into evidence. If not, I will leave them be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you whether or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then I would offer them, this particular document and we do have the supporting documents as well so that they can be carefully reviewed. This is our best work, though I hope there are no mistakes in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection to this document but we do object to the underlying judgements and the information there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question in relation to what is said just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Borovcanin, yesterday, the distinguished Mr. McCloskey also uttered a sentence namely your unit killed, et cetera. Please tell us, did your unit have an order, a command, in respect of these things that happened in the Kravica, in the forest, anywhere? Did your unit act as a unit involving command and control?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never issued that kind of order to anyone and I did not have any knowledge of any such thing happening at all, that it had happened or that it was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Borovcanin. Thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it again. You are now free to go. I also thank Ms. Cmeric for coming to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. President, and may I please be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I take it that the Defence is not tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that paragraph 13 is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, before you commence your evidence, Mr. Macar, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal will -- would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you, for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable and also let us speak slowly, both you and I, and let us pause between what we both have to say. Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D9110 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this statement before you now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be displayed for the witness so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers essentially be the same, like in this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps they would just be more extensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement according to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sutherland, except for the paragraph I referred to, i.e. paragraph 13?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Good morning. And no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit the Rule 92 ter statement with the redaction of paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3663, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Mr. Goran Macar's statement in English. [In English] Goran Macar was chief of the crime prevention department at the Sarajevo town Secretariat for the Interior, SUP, from spring 1990 to 3rd of April, 1992. When the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia was formed, he was appointed co-ordinator of operative work at the crime prevention and detection [Realtime transcript read in error "detention"] administration in the -- in late April. In October 1992, Mr. Macar organised the crime prevention and detection [Realtime transcript read in error "detention"] administration at the Republika Srpska MUP headquarters in Bijeljina. He was officially appointed chief of the administration on 13th of May, 1994. On 23rd of July, 1997, he was appointed chief of the SJB. From March 1998 to February 1999 he was a MUP employee without assignment. Goran Macar assisted the transformation of the police -- political situation and MUP structure and the victory of the national parties in the first multi-party -- after the victory of the national parties at the first multi-party elections. Parties became very influential in selecting the BH MUP staff and the SDA led the way in this. Within a new regime, ethnic origin became a determinant factor in personnel selections and overshadowed the importance of the quality criterion. The SDA raised a number of reserve police men against the rules, primarily appointing Muslims. Muslims were also appointed as commanders at the reserve police station where the Serb representatives -- they represented the majority and weapons were taken away and were distributed to the station -- to stations where Muslims were a majority. In general, Serbs were always given marginal tasks. In May 1991, the MUP and the state security had information that the SDA was working on creating paramilitary formations. The Green Berets were engaging well-known criminals in their ranks who mostly became commanders of their units. Toward the end of 1991 criminals were allowed to walk around Sarajevo freely and even go to the Stari Grad SUP SJB. Serbian policemens were threatened by the criminals and their Muslim colleagues and forced to leave the Stari Grad public security station. All attempts of Serbian policemen to do their work were thwarted by Muslim colleagues. The situation was similar in other parts of the BH. By the end of 1991, Croatian Defence forces HOS established check-points in different areas of BH. In early 1992, Croatian forces captured a group of policemen sent to assist the Bosanski Brod SJB in the fighting against arms smuggling. The smuggling of weapons from Croatia to BH had a scope of arming Muslims and Croats. All these incidents led to the disorganisation and the split of the MUP by ethnic groups. The goal of the Muslims was to take complete control of the MUP while the Serbs were trying to soften the SDS -- SDA domination and the Croats directed their influence toward the municipal structures in which they represented the majority. This sort of division also existed in the Serbian police. The police structure dissolved and its work became paralysed in January 1992. Check-points made up of members of the MUP active and reserve complements of the Green Berets were set up around Sarajevo. On 15th of March, 1992, the command of the school -- of the 2nd Army district was blocked. Thousands of civilians were there and active and reserve policemen bore rifles but did nothing to protect the command from the civilians. The Green Berets were also present. Negotiations were underway to divide the MUP into three parts. This division was meant to be based on the Cutileiro Plan. By the end of March the Croats had already set up a staff in Mostar that was responsible for the areas where the Croats were in the majority. At that time, I -- it was still not agreed how the Serbian MUP and the SB -- CSB would operate with regard to security. On 3rd of April, 1992, Goran Macar was forced to leave his job and flee Sarajevo because his name was in the list of the Serbian leading officials who the Muslim leadership wanted arrested. Three days later, Serbian policemen Pero Petrovic was killed at the Novo Sarajevo station. In those days, thousands of refugees flooded into Zvornik -- into Sokolac mostly from Gorazde and Sarajevo. On 19th of April, 1992, Goran Macar rejoined the RS MUP. The Serbian MUP was set up in Pale. Pale is a small town which means that it was not entirely suitable for MUP headquarters. It was overrun by the huge number of refugees and had problems with water, electricity and other basic provisions including communications. Information received was very incomplete. It was impossible to communicate with the SJBs but in the ARK until MUP headquarters moved to Bijeljina the administration only received 31 dispatches. Part of the administration located in Vraca was under constant artillery and sniper fire. There was also shortage of personnel, material and technical equipment. In the new organisation, the influence of local strongmen and the Crisis Staff on the SJB was enormous. They were the ones and not the ministry who appointed and paid the SJB chiefs and other policemen. Because of this, the SJBs did not report properly and fully to the ministry and it was not possible to establish proper subordination from the top downwards in the area of law and order. In addition, a number of SJBs had special units, later disbanded, which were neither directed nor approved by the ministry. In the second half of 1992, these units were disbanded and most of their members came under VRS command. Despite the scarcity of the staff and equipment, the RS MUP performed properly and fully respected RS laws. In this respect, all the ministers at the head of MUP were inexorable. Therefore members of the RS MUP did not behave differently depending on the ethnic origin of the perpetrators and the victims. They behaved in accordance with law. The non-existence of judicial organs, especially the prosecutor's office also affected the efficiency of the police. The police did not differentiate between ethnic origin of perpetrators or victims. Nevertheless, the RS MUP and the VRS had a widespread problem with the behaviour of volunteers, the Yellow Wasps were beyond all control. The VRS and MUP jointly disarmed it. The position of the MUP and the VRS was that only those armed formations envisaged by law could exist in the territory while those groups such as Yellow Wasps which were beyond the control were identified and prosecuted. Radovan Karadzic offered full support in solving all crimes and always emphasised the necessity to act in full compliance with the law. And that is a summary, and that moment I do not have questions for Mr. Macar. Although it is not an evidence but on page 16, line 17 to 19, I said that "detection" but it is recorded "detention," "detention."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

If we could go to the next document, please. utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Malko Koroman became chief before the 1st of April, 1992, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These documents that I have just shown you, Mr. Macar, show that, in fact, it was the RS MUP who were appointing - at least for the three examples that I've shown you -- appointing SJB chiefs in Prijedor, Sanski Most and Pale. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If you could put Mr. Zupljanin's document back up, in which he seeks approval, then we could proceed in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I don't intend doing that, Mr. Macar. The documents I've shown you show that these men were appointed with the approval of the Minister of the RS MUP to positions of chief of SJBs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't believe that Ms. Sutherland should be the one testifying. If she has a question she should put it and if the witness needs to refer to see a document he should be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, sorry, I said the three positions of CSBs. In fact the document on the screen signed by Mr. Stanisic is appointing Malko Koroman to SJB inspector in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you take a look at Mr. Zupljanin's memo or letter, as Mr. Macar requested?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is the second document, dated -- dated the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page 2 in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If I could see them again, because I noticed that these documents were not signed, either by Zupljanin or on his behalf and one more thing that's interesting is that the documents are dated at 30th of July, and they are referring to -- if I may read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, if I can interrupt you, it is signed, this document in front of us, in relation to Drljaca and it is simply post-dating something that has been -- that has taken place earlier. It says as of the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In order to discuss this decision, we must have the written approval in line with the procedures of the ministry, showing that the chief of the centre got approval to appoint someone. utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit them.

utterances.text: Exhibit P6379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you also said that the municipalities were paying the police. I want to show you a number of documents now in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25168, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The financing of public security stations and public security centres are not limited to the payment of salaries. utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.text: Perhaps you don't understand me. The funding of the police is not limited to salaries. utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The MUP headquarters, the MedFin service, provided money for the salaries but not for other expenses, and there was no SDK for the Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I put to you that this shows the money going through the channels down to the SJB, paying for salaries. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

This Trial Chamber has evidence before it in relation to the minister, Mico Stanisic, actually ordering his CSB chiefs and therefore the SJBs that report to the CSBs to report to them and collect information in relation to war crimes against Serbs. utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So this is -- is showing that the SJBs are to put emphasis on collecting crimes against Serb victims, yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I don't think it is true that they were to put a particular emphasis on it. I simply think that information was being gathered on crimes committed against the Serbs and that information was being sought in order to collate it. Due to a number of propaganda activities undertaken by the international media and the enemy side at the time, the situation was portrayed in a way as if there had been no crimes against the Serbs so we needed unified information on the plight of Serbs for government use. They were not particularly tasked with distinguishing between victims based on ethnicity, they were simply asked to forward information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will be able to read the document and draw a conclusion. If we could have 65 ter number 05664, this is the very short document dated the 15th of December and it's from Zoran Josic, department chief, and it's in relation to a dispatch, and it's saying: "Acting in accordance with your dispatch we have carried out the necessary checks and established that no crimes against the Serbian civilian population such as the crime of genocide and war crimes like the destruction of Orthodox cemeteries, churches and other cultural and historical monuments have been registered with the Banja Luka SJB."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So again, a dispatch is being given by CSB Banja Luka, it appears, and they are reporting -- the SJB is reporting back about the crimes against the Serbian civilian population, and in this case there are none. This is a -- another example of the MUP's focus on crimes where Serbs are the victims, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: It is not. This was simply another example of the continuous activity I just mentioned which was preparing information for the government, because some information was arriving late -- well, I'd like to see a dispatch, the dispatch, that they are referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't have that dispatch at my fingertips, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6384, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number -- sorry, Exhibit P02761.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, in fact it was the RS MUP who said that in its draft annual -- draft report for the work in the period of April to December 1992 that the focus was on the crimes committed by -- against the Serbian people. If we could go to page 15 of the English it's the second-to-last paragraph, and B/C/S it's page 21, also the second-to-last paragraph. And it says: "In this period the criminal inspectors visited all the CSBs and SJBs and had meetings where they gave instructions for carrying out concrete operative activities. The focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJB was on detection, documenting and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroy immovable property, cultural and religious monuments and other assets." Now, in early in 1993 you were directed to provide data in relation to Serb female victims only, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I don't recall it. If you were to show me a document, perhaps I could comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There are two documents that are related, 65 ter 25175 and 25174. If we could have the first one, 25175, it's dated the 1st of January, and it's an order from Mico Stanisic and it's to your attention and orders your service to make a list of the Serbian people -- it's actually from Todor Sikovic [phoen] but it's saying that the minister of the MUP, Mico Stanisic, has ordered that the service make a list of Serbian women who were raped by Muslim extremists based on the existing operational documentation. If we could have the second document, 65 ter 25174, this is dated two days later, again from the same person in the MUP detachment, to yourself and Dragan Kijac. And it says: "The vice-president of Republika Srpska, Biljana Plavsic, would like to know the extent to which the service has managed to implement the work of selecting the list of Serbian women raped by Muslim extremists." So did you provide this data?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Ms. Plavsic planned and organised a press conference in the international press centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your answer is non-responsive. I asked you whether you provided the data that -- that is a yes or a no answer. You either provided it or you didn't. Can you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As far as I recall, a list was not forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: But raped Serb women did attend an international press conference organised by Ms. Plavsic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, the focus of documenting crimes against the Serbian people continued right throughout the conflict, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Well, if we read the report you presented first, perhaps in one of the paragraphs we might be able to find something that is not fully in context with the paragraph you referenced. I think we reacted to the report where we were dissatisfied with the pace at which war crimes were being resolved, irrespective of the victims' ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 25185, please, this is a document from yourself to the Zvornik CJB dated the 17th of November, 1995. In view of the current events pertaining to the intense activity before the International Tribunal in The Hague and the attempts to tarnish the reputation of the Republika Srpska leadership, it is necessary for you to intensify activities in connection with preparing and filing criminal reports against perpetrators of war crimes against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So as I said a moment ago, this focus continued right throughout the conflict. We see here in November 1995, still the emphasis is on crimes against the Serbian people. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No, it is not. This dispatch had to do with gathering information on the plight of Serbs in the Drina region where the Srebrenica formations killed over 2.000 Serbs. The propaganda that was being put in place against the Serb people went so far as to have an international report of a scene where a mother is kissing the skull of her son, and perhaps if you allow me I'll tell you why it was done unless you don't want me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I actually do not want you to tell me about that. You just mentioned that a number of Serbs were killed around this time period. This is four months after thousands of men and boys from Srebrenica were summarily executed. As head of the crime administration weren't you just a little bit interested in documenting crimes that had been committed against the non-Serb population in this very area you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The minister of the interior dealt with documenting crimes it had information of having taken place, and it dealt with what was within the competence of the Ministry of the Interior. It did not involve itself in such affairs as to -- as such as the ones that belonged to the military domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're sending this document to the -- the Zvornik CJB. Now, in this document, you could have put, Prepare and file criminal reports against perpetrators of war crimes against all ethnicities, but you didn't, you chose to do it against crimes against the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I believe I tried to explain a moment ago what the reason was for drafting this dispatch. It wasn't drafted by me but by an inspector from my administration. I tried to explain what the reason was for its dispatch. The reason was the propaganda --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, no, no. I don't want you to repeat your answer you've just given. I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I had no time to provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, if he feels necessary. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no background context to this dispatch. It was created as a result of a propaganda broadcast on TV, where as proof of Serbian crimes, the viewers could see footage from a Serb village in the Drina region. A mother was filmed as kissing the skull of her own son and yet she was portrayed as the mother of a Muslim victim killed by Serbs. One of the cameramen, because the footage ended up in archives, in consultation with his bosses, provided additional information so that we could inform the public about the true nature of it and to document the rest of the crimes. There is no other background to this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 14, the witness said, "one of the inspectors," rather than "one of the cameramen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I want to now ask you about how the RS MUP actually investigated serious crimes against non-Serbs. You know that the Koricanske Stijene massacre which involved the killing of around 150 to 200 men on Mount Vlasic on the 21st of August, 1992, you're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When -- when was it that you first became aware of this horrendous incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I became aware of it for the first time, I think, in September 1992 when I was working on preparing for the move to the new ministry seat in Bijeljina. I think it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you do as -- as a de facto head of this crime detention and prevention administration in relation to the investigation into the massacre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The minister of the interior, Mr. Stanisic, once he received information of this crime, sent a dispatch, an order, asking for the most emphatic investigation to be conducted by the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm asking whether you did anything in relation to it. I don't want to know about the details about what Banja Luka had to do. I'm simply wanting to focus on -- on what you did. If I can -- if I can just say, Tomo Kovac, who was the assistant minister for police affairs from August 1992 through September 1993, testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial that as the crime enforcer at the time you were in charge of the activities taken place -- taking place at the time and he said that at transcript page 27106. What were those activities that you were involved in -- that you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be placed on the screen to see whether Tomo Kovac said so with regards to the Koricanske Stijene incident or in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. 65 ter 25165, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see here that Mr. Kovac is asked about 120 and 200 Muslims being taken off a bus, lined up along the edge of the cliff and machine-gunned. And he was asked if he knew about that crime and he said he found out subsequently, and in his answer to when he was asked when he first learned about it, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we have that page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm reading from line -- I'm just about to get to line 7 to 12. And when he's asked when he first learned about it, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You read from the first line, very well, yes. Please continue. But read slow, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he said: "I don't know. I cannot state with certainty when I exactly heard it for the first time but I was not involved in any actions taken by the ministry with regard to that and therefore cannot comment on the exact time when I learned about it. The chief of crime enforcement at the time, Goran Macar, was in charge of the activities taken at the time. That much I know. But I couldn't give you any additional details."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Macar, what activities were you in charge of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry to see that there was no text in the Serbian. At the time of the event itself, I was co-ordinator for operational affairs in the crime police administration at the seat of the ministry. In August and partly September, I worked on one specific task, which was an operation that was being carried out against the group called the Yellow Wasps. Only in early October or actually in late September, was I tasked by Mr. Stanisic as well as authorised by him, to set up the crime police administration in the headquarters. As you well know, for as long as the administration was in Pale, it only had a few inspectors, and was not set up per se. Its proper setup activities were only undertaken once we were in Bijeljina when I was authorised to create a crime department -- the crime administration in the headquarters of the ministry, from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So your short answer to that is you did nothing in relation to Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar you are with the organisation of the Ministry of the Interior but you should be familiar. The competence for shedding more light on various incidents according to the Law on the Interior and the Law on Criminal Procedure is in the centre of security services in Banja Luka, and they are supposed to act in relation to that kind of incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you mentioned in your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony that two or three perpetrators had been identified but that they were at the front line. I think that I'm not going to call the document up, that's D01882 of the 9th of September from Simo Drljaca. If you're head of this crime prevention and detention [sic] administration -- you said that you -- in Stanisic/Zupljanin you said that you went to Banja Luka in March 1993, seven months after the crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If you read the statement carefully, and I believe that you did, you could have noticed that after the basic configuration was established for the administration at headquarters, in November 1992, mid-November, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but my question was you went to Banja Luka in March 1993; is that right? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I can answer the question. I was in Banja Luka both in March and in November, and one is linked to the other as well as to your statement, What did you do over those seven months. It would only be proper for me to respond, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, let me put it like this: If -- if there was information in September that there were two people -- two or three people named who were part of the traffic police that were assisting this convoy get through get through Mount Vlasic, and at that point, from -- from September through till -- through till March, nothing is being done, don't you think that -- that it's -- how hard would it have been for anyone in the RS MUP or the investigative judge, in fact, even, to pick up the -- the phone to the -- to the corps command and say, We want these people back from the front?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: What's the question, after all of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That nothing was done, nothing, nothing at all was done about trying to identify the perpetrators to this crime.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: That is your assertion. The centre of public security that is supposed to act, in charge of acting, they carried out checks and activities related to the identification, that is to say starting with the on-site investigation up to identification in accordance with the law. If you're asking me whether I personally took part in the actual operations involved, no, I did not because it was not my job to do that. I -- may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: At the end of September, I was given the task to set up the crime police administration at the seat of the ministry. That does not mean that the centre of public security in Banja Luka was not doing its own work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, when you went there in November, knowing that they had this -- sorry, in March. You said that you went there in March and -- and this is at transcript page 25387, you said -- you were asked, when in March when you were informed -- when you went to talk about the status of the Koricanske Stijene case were you briefed, were you presented a report, or did you inspect the files of the crime police of Banja Luka CSB? You said, No, I didn't inspect the files. I was briefed by the relevant officer of the crime service there. Now, knowing that nothing had taken place in seven months in trying to establish the identity of these perpetrators when everyone knew that it was the police that were involved, didn't you think it was incumbent upon you and your administration to go through the files in Banja Luka, to go through the files in Prijedor, perhaps find the pay lists for August 1992 for the -- for the police, start interviewing those people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In order to view the situation better, and in order for it not to appear as if we had been passive, I have to remind you of something. The representatives of the crime police administration in mid-November 1992 went to Banja Luka. I was there, too, together with a few inspectors. Information about crime was supposed to be one of the subjects dealt with, and that included the Koricanske Stijene file as well. You have my statement that I gave in the Stanisic case. You could see that no meeting took place because of certain technical omissions of the leading people at the Security Services Centre. Also, we can see from that statement that we proceeded to Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, if I can stop you there. You -- you actually -- because of, as you say, a technical omission, either between Stojan Zupljanin or Djuro Bulic who was the deputy, you didn't get to speak to the -- to the chief of whoever you wanted to speak to but there were other people within that crime administration department in Banja Luka that you could have spoken to and you chose not to. And then you -- and then you -- you left to go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No. The meeting did not take place. Everybody from the centre was doing their own job. Also, we had these financial constraints, I mean spending a few days in Banja Luka, you can see that from a series of our reports and that's why we proceeded to Prijedor because the plan was for us to go to Prijedor on that same day. We planned time in accordance with the resource that we had in terms of our stay in the area. Unfortunately, the meeting was not held. As you can see from my statement in the Stanisic case it wasn't held in Prijedor either, because of what Mr. Drljaca did, I explained that in that statement, and we returned without completing our mission. We returned to Bijeljina. And the next time I went to the Banja Luka centre was in March, and then I asked to receive information about the crime situation in the territory of the centre inter alia about the Koricanske Stijene file. That was not supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you didn't -- you didn't ask -- you didn't look at any of the files, you simply received a briefing from the officer that was present there. And from that point on, even in March 1993, nothing is done in relation to this case until even -- to even to the end of the conflict in 1995 and more, and then in 1999 the RS authorities begin to pick it up again and then still nothing. And it's not until the -- the prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2003 actually do something about it when they issue indictments against these people, and of course the ICTY had issued an indictment against one of the perpetrators that was in the Intervention Platoon in the Prijedor police. So when you went there in -- in 1993, in March, and you said, Oh, something has to be done, nothing was done, and you didn't, it appears, do anything to follow it up. And you're supposed to be the head of the crime prevention and detention -- detection administration.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm saying isn't it right that you -- nothing was done about this case until the police prosecutor in Bosnia issued indictments in 2003 and the ICTY did something about it when they issued their indictment against one of the police involved?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I don't know what the BH Prosecutor's office did. However, had you not interrupted me you could have heard, and you also have that in my statement, in March when I went to visit the Banja Luka centre from the then-head of the crime police and other top personnel were present, I was informed about what they had done in that case. I received information then, and as I said in my previous statement I cannot recall exactly, there were a few suspects, two, four, six, eight, I cannot really say what the figures would be, and allegedly they were fugitives and they were somewhere in the army. Also, I was informed that they established contact with the military police, once they received this kind of information, and they asked for these persons to be brought into custody. I absolutely received no information on the basis of which I would have any doubts regarding what that person had told me. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I would like to move on. You mentioned a moment ago that when you were -- in August of 1992 you were -- you were in Bijeljina investigating the Yellow Wasps. You were -- you sent a report back to the RS minister on the 4th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P02904, please -- oh, I'm sorry, I need 65 ter number 1D03658 first. And, Your Honour, that document that was just on the screen, the page of transcript from Stanisic/Zupljanin, I don't intend to tender because it was the -- the relevant passage was read into the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this is the cover letter to Mico Stanisic, isn't it, that -- that you -- you forwarded the statements and -- and a report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender this -- I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6386, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have P0290 -- start again. P02904. It's P02904.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, this is a report -- you're familiar with this report, aren't you, Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in fact, you said in Stanisic/Zupljanin that this was an unsigned report which was produced by employees of the crime prevention administration and in part by personnel from the Bijeljina SJB who took part in the procedure, and that was at transcript page 2300 -- 000. If we could go to page 4 of -- the last page, please, the last paragraph of the report, it mentions that information obtained by the Serb armed forces military police and the MUP national security operatives indicate that Dusan Vukovic, aka Repic, was committing massacre-genocide over civilians of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the Muslim ethnicity. And then you said verification and materialisation of these informations was being taken care of by the Serb armed forces military police in co-operation with the MUP international security operatives. Now, given that you were aware of this information that they were involved in serious crimes against civilians, why then was the criminal charges that were raised by Andan, why did they only include car theft and not allegations about these crimes that had been committed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As is well known to the Prosecution, I know that you have that documentation as well, as for this group, it is the military security organs that were supposed to deal with them and the military Prosecutor's office. I personally did not take part in planning this operation of disarming and arresting them and planning further activities. Had I taken part in that, my proposal would have been the following: The Ministry of the Interior, the crime prevention employees should be helping the military security organs in shedding more light on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I stop you there? Your answer, I think, is non-responsive. I asked you why did it only -- why did the criminal charges only include car theft and not these allegations of which the MUP were aware of. That was my question, not about anything to do with an operation to arrest these people. I'm asking you about the criminal charges that were filed after they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If you would please be so kind as to allow me to finish, then you would understand that that is an answer to your question, and what I was saying was in that context actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please try to answer in a simpler manner, yes. At times you didn't answer the question. That's why Ms. Sutherland interrupted a couple of times. Let's go back to the question. Could you put your question again, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, why -- why were not allegations about the involvement of certain individuals in crimes committed against the civilian non-Serb population, why were they not included in the criminal charges which were raised against these people, in addition to the grand larceny of a number of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The commission of crimes of any kind by these perpetrators was within the jurisdiction of the military and that's what I've been trying to tell you. Even what the -- even the crimes that the police had dealt with, it was the military security organs that were supposed to deal with this and the military Prosecutor's office. That's why I said if I had taken part in this operation, it wouldn't have been the police that would have brought charges against these people. We would have helped the military organs to prosecute and deal with the matter. Because this kind of crime would be within the jurisdiction of the military Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. We will get to that in one moment but we just need --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session for just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Repic [sic], I also want to show you another statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I note that you spent all the time allotted to you. The Chamber will take a break now for 20 minutes, after which I would expect you to conclude within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 12.13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I have a bit of a faux pas, I called you Mr. Repic just before the break. I apologise. If we could have 65 ter 25203, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I accept your apology.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a statement dated the 4th of August, 1992, taken by the military police. It's an official note after interviewing Dusko Vukovic, aka Repic. He then makes the following statement, and in it, in paragraph 2 at the bottom of the -- the last paragraph on page 1, going over on to page 2, and in the B/C/S on page 2, the second paragraph -- no, page 1, sorry -- no, at page 2 of the B/C/S, starting, "We were taken to the Sabac prison." Just down into that paragraph: "Until the 10th of June, 1992, I wandered aimlessly around Zvornik and then I heard about a prison for Muslims at Celopek. I went to Celopek on the same day and got into the prison for Muslims who had been arrested at Divic." And then he talks about what he does, "I organised a boxing match between the prisoners in the hall, gave them bats to hit each other. He got bored with that and then he took a small-calibre rifle which an acquaintance of his was carrying and fired 15 shots into the prisoners. I finished off some of the wounded prisoners by stabbing them in the heart with a knife, and I cut the ears off some."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow, slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [As read] "And I cut the ears off some. I don't remember the exact number of people that I did this to." And then he goes on, "After killing several prisoners, I called the reserve policeman-guards to find a truck and ordered four Muslims to load the bodies of the dead prisoners on the truck. After that, I went with two reserve policemen to a gravel pit and made the four Muslims unload the bodies after which the reserve policemen were shot and killed them." Now, he says that he thinks there were two people with him and names them there in this statement. Now, Mr. Macar, this is -- this is information involving or alleging that reserve policemen were involved in this incident with Repic. Why weren't -- why wasn't an investigation made in relation to -- in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I see this statement for the first time. I don't know if it was presented in the Stanisic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it was it was presented to you in the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: All right. But anyway, it wasn't forwarded to the MUP staff. And if you had let me finish earlier, when I was saying that I took part in the planning of activities, the planning in which I took part would have been led by the military police in co-operation with the staff of our ministry, and not on two separate tracks. At that time, it was not forwarded to us, nor was this done later, so that we could plan and take some measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Macar, I just need to make a correction to the transcript. On page 18 -- line 18 on page 54 -- or line 17: After that I went to two reserve policemen to a gravel pit and made the Muslims -- and the four Muslims unload the bodies after which the reserve policemen were shot and killed them. It actually says, "... where the reserve policemen shot and killed them." I'm sorry. In any event, Mr. Macar, you knew about the -- the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 55, in line 6, the witness said, "If I had taken part, it would have been this way or that," so not that "I took part" but "had I taken part."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you were heading up this -- this investigation, were you not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In the segment that was assigned to the crime police, and we were sent to the SJB in Bijeljina to help them out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said after the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar you're being asked to repeat the -- repeat your answer after the first sentence -- after the first sentence, where you said: "In the segment that was assigned to the crime police, and we were sent to the SJB in Bijeljina to help them out." The interpreters haven't caught what you said after that point but -- so can you please go on from there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: According to the agreement between the representatives of the MUP and the military police, we were in charge of some things and that's what we did. It was mostly crimes against property. And the information that we may have obtained in interviewing those deprived of liberty, we forwarded to the military police. Information of this kind was never received from the military bodies, at least I did not, and I was the head of that crime police group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, we just looked at P02905 which was the report that you annexed to the cover letter that you sent to Stanisic, in that last paragraph it said the military police and the MUP are aware that genocide was being committed against the Muslims. So you had information at your fingertips that MUP -- that crimes were being committed. And why didn't you further investigate those crimes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I believe I answered this question earlier. Crimes, and I mean all crimes committed by this group, was in the remit of military bodies, that is the military police and the military Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This -- this statement, Mr. Repic's statement clearly says that reserve policemen were guards at Celopek were involved in crimes. Now, as -- as -- as a head of the administration, it's incumbent upon you to follow up with crimes against civilians, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I don't know if my previous statement has been correctly interpreted to you. I think so. I said that the statement taken by the military from the person in question was never forwarded to the MUP -- or, rather, the representative of the MUP working on that case. We had separate facilities. There was a group in the SJB of Bijeljina and there was the military police, and the military Prosecutor's office had their own facilities, separate ones. We never got this information so as to be able to act upon it. We never received it either orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is evidence that you knew that that crimes had been committed and if -- and if the military police were not doing anything about it, your police, the civilian police, should have taken the matter up and investigated it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Although you're insisting, we hadn't -- had no access to information about what the military bodies were doing, that is the military police, the military prosecutor's office, based on which we may have known that somebody weren't doing their job. The military police or the military prosecutor's office never briefed us about their activities, nor was it part of our remit, nor could we control them or their actions under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke a moment ago when I said it was Exhibit P2905, it's in fact P2904. Then why do you put in this report that the information obtained by the Serb armed forces military police and the MUP national security operatives indicate that Dusan Vukovic, aka Repic, was committing a massacre? So you are aware that he was -- he was involved in crime against -- crimes against non-Serbs. So you keep saying that you're not -- you weren't aware of this particular statement but then how come in the bottom of your report you say that you're aware of crimes committed by him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If you listened carefully, or perhaps my sentences are long and therefore not so easy to follow, it is beyond doubt that we had information that Repic had committed some crimes. We didn't have specific information saying that he did this or that in place X or Y. But that was all in the remit of the military police and the military security bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in P2904 that you've got information that he committed crimes against Muslims in Celopek. That's exactly what he says he's doing in this statement. I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Macar, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. First of all, the witness ought to be able to answer the question which wasn't really a question but was some testimony by Ms. Sutherland, but he ought to be able to comment on it before we move on. Secondly, we object to the statement because the witness hasn't confirmed anything, and it doesn't contradict his testimony as there is no evidence that he would have been expected to have -- this to have come into his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it goes to the witness's credit. He said that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it go to the credibility of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because he said he sent P2904 to Mico Stanisic. In P2904 it states exactly that -- that Dusan Vukovic, aka Repic, is involved in crimes in Celopek. This statement of Repic's says exactly that. And so it's whether you want to believe this witness when he says that he wasn't aware of this [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sp my question is: Does it bolster his credibility? Or it contradicts his [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It contradicts his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How? How?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well -- it -- it's whether you believe him when he says that he hasn't received this statement. You can draw an inference from --
