utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your case that this document says that he received this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm saying that the information contained in 65 ter 25203 is exactly the information that is contained in P904 about the facts of -- of -- of Dusan Vukovic, aka Repic, committing crimes in Celopek. Now, whether this witness is to be believed as to whether he was aware of this statement is -- is a matter for you, and I'm saying that -- that you should have this evidence in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I would like ask this document to be identified. Whose military police is this? Is there a number? Is there a signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. We will not admit this. And I'm seeing the clock. How many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had two topics, one question on one topic and a couple of very brief questions on the other topic, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, in paragraph 31 of your statement you said that you were present at several meetings where Dr. Karadzic was also present. When was the very first meeting you had with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I remember that meeting well. I don't believe Mr. Karadzic would remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just have the date? Can I just have the time period not the details of the meeting? I just want the date first.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The first contact with Mr. Karadzic was in April, probably in the second half of April 1992. And that was when I first met Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And were -- at this meeting were specific cases discussed, for example, Arkan's group, Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No. Mr. Koljevic was present at that meeting, then Mr. Buha, Mr. Ostojic and some other people. I believe that Mrs. Plavsic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the -- sorry, when was the next meeting? You said you were present at several meetings. When was the next meeting after this meeting in second half of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I'm now pressing backwards based on memory. I was there in 1994, in 1993, 1992. I think this was the only meeting that I attended. But in 1993, 1994 and in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Even, if I may assist you, in 1994 I called a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'm interested in meetings that you had with him in 1992 and you mentioned the one in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to now, because of time, move on to my last topic and that is about -- you said a number of SJBs had some sort of special units which were neither directed nor approved by the ministry and were against regulations. Are you confining it to -- you mention SJBs but do you confine it to SJBs only or do you include also special units at the regional level? Because also in paragraph 20 you say later in the second half of 1992 these units were disbanded and most of their numbers came under the VRS command. So my question is, is it -- are you confining it only to SJB special units or are you also talking about units -- special units, at the regional level?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Not all stations had that kind of staff but there were some --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, it's a yes or a no answer. Are you confining it to SJBs or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: There were some with the centres too, not only the stations but also the public security centres, not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that they were -- were neither approved by the ministry -- or they were neither directed or approved by the ministry; right? I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do not overlap with the translation. I'm not sure the witness understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I just see the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You just mentioned just then that you were in -- in -- in addition to the SJBs you were also including in this statement that you make in paragraph 20 that it also includes special units at the regional level. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so I want to know whether you were present when -- well, I'll go back a moment. Zupljanin established a special unit in early May 1992. I see you smirking. That's documented in D01536. And there was an official parade held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992, to celebrate the creation of this unit at which Minister Stanisic attended along with Zupljanin, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Brdjanin and the RS deputies. Were you present that day when -- at the official parade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if there was this parade in front of the minister along with Karadzic, Krajisnik and others, then it appears to be approval by the minister, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection. It's calling for speculation. He already said he wasn't there. He's not an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why does he need an expertise to answer this question? If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the basis for him to answer this question in any -- he's simply a member of the ministry being asked to comment on something he wasn't present at or didn't have any knowledge of, at least so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So as a member of the ministry, would you agree that such parade could not be conducted without the approval of the minister?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's fair enough to ask that question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If there was a parade of a special unit or maybe a police parade, the police of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we must distinguish. If it was a parade of the Special Police, certainly he knew, but we must identify whether it was a parade of the police, which at that time got uniforms and insignia and so on, which could have been a parade of the police of the public security station or the centre or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I don't have time to play you the videotape but in the beginning of the rally, the parade, Mr. Zupljanin says: "Respectful ladies and gentlemen, dear country men and prominent guests, I have the pleasure to greet and thank you for coming to give importance to this humble celebration of marking the 13th of May --" sorry, I misspoke a moment ago, "The day of the security organs and services when we promote the police insignia of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the promotion of the special detachment of the CSB Banja Luka." And then he greets all the guests, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Milan Martic, Boro Djukic, Mico Stanisic, Cedo Kljajic, Momo Mandic and all the deputies and guests of the session. Another name which is Stojan Spanojevic [phoen], I think. So it is in relation to the police and in particular the CSB special detachment, special unit. So are you able to, in answer to the question --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: If this has nothing to do with the Special Police, that's a question I cannot answer but I know that Minister Stanisic demanded that all units established in the first half or, rather, from April until July or August 1992, be disbanded. I was present at the parade at Sokolac on the 30th of March. It was a promotion of uniforms in the Krajina and the insignia, but I don't have information whether Special Police was established in Banja Luka. So I couldn't comment. I know of some other cases, but I cannot confirm if the special unit was at the parade and if anybody heard Stojan Zupljanin say that he had a special unit. Anyway, it doesn't mean that he was established with the approval of the minister. I'm afraid I cannot make a comment that could shed more light on what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'll just follow up on one thing that you said about attending that Sokolac parade on the 30th of March. You -- you testified in Stanisic/Zupljanin, did you not, that -- that it wasn't only Sokolac police, it was for the autonomous region of Romanija, and that there was also people there, police officers from Ilijas and Pale. And that was on the 30th of March, 1992, which was -- which was one day before Momo Mandic sent out the dispatch saying there is going to be an RS MUP. That -- that's the Sokolac parade that you're talking about that you attended, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you did say that it was not only Sokolac police but also Pale and Ilijas police forces were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes. There was also a parade of the police of public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And my final question is: And these same special units that you just said a moment ago were disbanded by -- on the minister's instruction, was that the same special units that were awarded commendations by Karadzic in November 1993 and you were shown that document in -- in Stanisic/Zupljanin, the list, P092978? Is that the same special units you're talk about that were disbanded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The composition cannot have been the same, and there were transformations in all those units. I really can't remember if anybody from the original composition of the unit who remained afterwards, because I really didn't know these people, and I wasn't in charge of special units anyway. I don't know if I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I thank you very much for the indulgence of the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I have a few questions and I will start with the latest topic from page 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Macar, were these the only units of the Special Police or were they the PJP units, and was there a special unit at the level of the ministry which existed with the approval and was created by the minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: At the level of the ministry, there was a detachment of the Special Police commanded by Mr. Milenko Karisik. It was the only regular unit established with the approval of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether I praised that unit or the ones that were disbanded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I know you commended the unit commanded by Mr. Karisik. You reminded me now, perhaps that's what Madam Prosecutor had in mind when she mentioned the transformation, that unit was transformed in 1993. It was split into five parts. From that unit, dislocated companies were established in the centres, in Bijeljina, Banja Luka, Sarajevo and Trebinje. So it was a result of the transformation of that unit. It had nothing to do with the units from Banja Luka or any other location. By that time, General Saric was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was stated that on the 13th of May, there was a parade of either that unit or that it was present during the security day celebrations. Do you know when the security day was established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The 13th of May holiday is something that existed in the previous regime, and we chose a different day to celebrate the Ministry of the Interior which is the 4th of April. The 13th of May remained from the previous regime. It was a holiday of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could Minister Stanisic have as early as the 13th of May, 1992, information and evidence that the units that existed were inadequate and should be disbanded?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No, in no case. And not only pertaining to those units, we did not receive regular information from the field as per Serb-held municipalities. We didn't even receive information from the respective security stations and CSBs. All communication was down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested that the police parade took place on the 30th of March. Do you know what the date was when the Assembly of the Serbian People session was held, when the decision on the implementation of the Cutileiro Plan was reached regarding the police as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: It was in March, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it before the 30th, before the parade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was before the parade. I recall that because my then-superior, Mr. Jozo Leutar, told me that there would be a transformation within the MUP and it would be split into three parts. He also said that the Croats had already established their headquarters in Mostar and that they were working on equipping their force in keeping with the Cutileiro Plan. That is why I remember that the parade took place after the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the Cutileiro Plan and certain arrangements within the MUP, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you drafted your report and sent it to Minister Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Repic -- was he at large at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I can't recall whether he was still at large but he -- in any case, he was unavailable in the course of the first few days. I don't know whether he was held by the military police, though. In any case, he wasn't among those who were brought to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the document number you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is P029024, which was used a few times today. It is Mr. Macar's report to the Minister Stanisic -- to Minister Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, do you remember when the arrest of the Yellow Wasps was carried out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The Yellow Wasps were arrested, I think, in late July, up to the 1st of August, I think. That's when it was completed. On the 3rd of August, I arrived with the group in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 46, you were asked about what was done and what was not done concerning the investigation of crimes. Can you tell us this: When was an investigating judge made part of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The investigating judge was included only once the judiciary was established in Republika Srpska. In the specific case of Koricanske Stijene, there was an investigating judge as well as a prosecutor and a military prosecutor, and the investigating judge was in charge of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 48 you mentioned a chief of the crime service from the Banja Luka centre. Can you explain to us what administrations existed within the MUP and how far did the lines within the organisation go, if they existed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: There was a crime police administration, the uniformed police administration -- apologies, the communications administration, and encoding administration, the personnel and legal affairs administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us stay with your administration.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, there was also the administration for materiel and financial affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to your administration, your service, were there any lines which went down and how far down did it go?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Within the administration, in late 1992, we established a line for white-collar crime, general crime, and later on there was a department to combat drugs traffic -- trafficking. In the CSBs, there was a sector or department for crime prevention and they had their groups for general crime, white-collar crime, and scene-of-crime officers. In the seat of the administration it was only in 1993 that we established a scene of crime centre. In the public security stations, there were smaller groups of inspectors who had one or no scene-of-crime officers, which was the case particularly at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of investigating crimes within or inside that line?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: All investigating procedures were in charge of -- were tasked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly start again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer? Start -- please start over again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness approach the microphone as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my back. That's why I pulled back. Apologies. Public security stations dealt with such crimes which were within the remit of the municipal and district prosecutor's offices. All crimes committed by unidentified perpetrators were part of the public security station remit. Financial crime or white-collar crime, that was within the remit of the CSBs. Public security stations dealt mainly with property climbs and small-scale crimes, petty crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that you did not carry out supervision in November through March in the Banja Luka CSB. What did you mean by that? And was the administration in charge of investigating from its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: As for supervision in 1992 and 1993, we did not carry it out in any CSB or station. First of all, we did not have enough personnel and we did not have materiel and equipment which would enable us to visit all CSBs and stations. Supervising a CSB takes at least between 10 and 15 days, we did not have people or means to be in a particular centre for 15 days in order to carry out supervision, which is also something that you can see from our reports and collegium meetings that are available to both the Prosecution and Defence because I mentioned a few times that we were short of resources in terms of personnel and supplies and that I could not send out inspectors in the field unless properly equipped by the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the level of the ministry and the administration in the headquarters, were investigations carried out that were otherwise within the remit of stations and CSBs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Only in exceptionally on minister's orders could the inspectors from the crime prevention administration go to CSBs or stations to assist with particular cases. I would also like to add that in the CSB of Banja Luka they had better personnel in terms of numbers and training to deal with those issues. We barely had a minimum correspondence to carry out communication between CSBs, the ministry and stations. We also rarely went out into the field in order to acquaint ourselves with the security station in the CSBs and stations, in order have a full picture of the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you understand my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For planning purpose I'd like to know how much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think around ten minutes, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue after lunch break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is okay with the witness we'll then continue ten minutes and then conclude this witness's evidence. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there casualties among Serb civilians in the federal part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and did you have access in order to carry out investigations of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: We gathered and received information but we couldn't carry out investigations in that part of the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 33, it was suggested that you issued tasks with regard to collecting information on crimes over Serb civilians. Does gathering information equal carrying -- the carrying out of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: No. Let me expand on this and I would have done so had I been allowed by Madam Prosecutor. Large population migrations took place from the Muslim and Croat-held territory to the Serb-controlled territory. There were hundreds of thousands of people who had information about the events from towns and municipalities they hailed, and we had to talk to them and gather information about the events and crimes, et cetera. That is why we placed a particular stress on it, on several occasions. A large number of that population went on through to Serbia and we were afraid they would become unavailable so we strove to carry out as many conversations and interviews as possible while they were still in our part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you understand my position vis-a-vis investigating crimes committed against Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principal, whenever I attended any meetings you asked most emphatically to discover the perpetrators of all crimes. You also stressed the importance of shedding light on crimes against the non-Serb population both from the point of view of the reputation of Republika Srpska and in terms of possible reactions of the public. To add on to something that I was asked by Madam Prosecutor, in 1993 I think it was in October, in the first part of October, there was a meeting in Pale which I initiated, where the RS Prosecutor was in attendance as well as the president of the military prosecutor's office, representatives of the Main Staff and the Ministry of Justice. The topic was working on dealing with war crimes and the flow of information. I remember you came in to greet all those present and you asked very energetically that all should do their utmost to speed up the detection of discovery perpetrators of such crimes irrespective of the ethnic background of either the perpetrators or victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, was there any cover-up of crimes irrespective of whether the perpetrator was known and available or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I'll start with myself. Since I began working for the service, I never asked anyone to cover up or commit a crime. We also did not have information that anyone from the public security stations or CSBs was covering up and holding back information on certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If everything was documented, what happened with this process of documenting crimes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: The biggest problem was in 1992, so let's start from the beginning. In most of the RS territory, there were no Prosecutor's offices, no courts, no military prosecutor's offices or military courts. It was only in the second part of the year that we saw the establishment of some. And in October, there were certain personnel changes because certain people in positions of -- and Prosecutor's offices could not get their bearings. Much of the material that was gathered simply sat there and was not sent to the judiciary. As regards the process of documenting, and the documents we sent to the Prosecutor's offices, and those that were still being processed, many of those files were not concluded because information on the perpetrators was mostly unknown. Such material was then left within the respective centres and stations. After the war, as I could see myself, members of SFOR, I don't know whether they Prosecution representatives with them, but I saw them gather and seize documents under threat of weapons. I saw it in 1997 in the Sarajevo centre. They simply drive you out of your office and take what they need. We could not know what they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I did not even know whether they displayed on CDs what they took away then because there were boxes, packages, it was very hard to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 23 today, what was put to you was a document from the 30th of July, 1992. And this document confirms that Simo Drljaca was appointed on the 29th of April, 1992. Can you tell us how come there is this three-month difference and can you tell us whether there had been a decision before this decision and who made this decision on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I'm convinced that the Ministry of the Interior -- rather, the minister, did not give his consent for this decision. Why it was done in July to cover this period, I don't know. Because what is logical is, what was displayed here as well, of course it's necessary to have the consents of the minister. The minister would always give his consent or approval in writing never just by saying so. If consent was given, then there has to be a written document that should be provided to the security centre or to the organ where a particular person is being appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What comes first and what comes second? Consent and then employment or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: First there has to be a request from the organ involved, that is looking for a particular person to take a job, and then certain requirements have to be met and then the minister is supposed to provide his consent. There is a decision on approval that has to be made, and I think that the legal affairs department in 1992 pointed out these problems that were occurring on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as I can remember, the OTP has this information in the Stanisic file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't catch the date. Did you talk about the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime towards the end of 1992, the department for personnel and legal affairs compiled a paper in terms of how people were being employed, not only top personnel but police personnel in general. And they -- they looked at these cases, if you will, when people were admitted without the consent of the ministry. Individual cases were not referred to there but it was the problem that was indicated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned something and then you were interrupted. During the first few months, there was no system of payments with the Krajina that was functioning. What did you -- what were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I was trying to say that the ministry could not even pay salaries, and the autonomous region then paid their salaries, and what is the most important thing is that is not the salaries only, when I'm speaking of payments, but all the material resources that were provided by the municipalities to the centre and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned on page 33 -- or, rather, a document was mentioned, P6383, that there was no cash available. Can you tell us how come that happened? How come there was no cash? Was there a shortage of cash, and if so why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Well, of course, when there was no system of payments in place, and in this state of war, transactions as such were brought to a halt and everything that happened. I mean people were just using cash for payments, for suppliers and so on. So of course, dinars went outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was it being printed for new quantities to be made available?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at the office of the national bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question: A few documents regarding payments were put to you. And this had to do with paragraph 20 of your statement. So please do take that statement of yours, it's the last sentence, or the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the document that fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are not following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Read slow, please. Very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 20, these sorts of things were most common in the ARK. This somewhat changed for the better when the Crisis Staffs and autonomous districts were dissolved. Can you tell us whether you remember when the Crisis Staffs were abolished?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in September or October. I think it was September 1992, around there, that would be the period. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We believe it's earlier than that, but we'll leave it at that. Thank you, Mr. Macar. Oh, I beg your pardon, I do apologise. Please, you were asked about the Yellow Wasps. So 1D9403, could we briefly take a look at that. Could you tell us what the attitude was of the MUP specifically towards that group, what was the position of the police vis-a-vis that group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Undeniably the position was that this was a group that was a renegade group, that was not under military control. So from Zvornik, Vlasenica, these stations sent information to the minister and then the minister to the government and probably to you, too. So this was the view both of the ministry and of the military that the Yellow Wasps and similar groups should be either disarmed or placed under control, if these are volunteers that they should be transported out into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at this document? First of all, it was addressed to the crime department and then to national security, and so on. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is? Read if first, please, and then tell us whether you received it, your department.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this document. At the end of 1992, there was a situation when border checks were better on our border. As for the Yellow Wasps, they were wanted for a while, two or three of them, I cannot remember exactly, and now the station is providing information to the following, that around 2330 hours, they set out and they wanted to get into Republika Srpska and they probably reacted, and together with the police they returned them to Serbia regarding the problems that they had had with them already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any bans on entering Republika Srpska on these grounds? Did you know about that? Did the MUP ban certain people from entering?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember any bans. The MUP can react vis-a-vis persons who are wanted persons, and if these are larger groups, of course their movements will be monitored, where they are going, why they are going there, but I do not remember a ban on entry quite literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out loud the first paragraph because we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: You mean this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: "On the 21st of November, 1992, around 2330 hours, at the border crossing Sepak, from the direction of Loznica, a group of organised volunteers tried to enter Republika Srpska. These persons are mostly members of the paramilitary formation called the Yellow Wasps or Zuco's men. In agreement with the police of Yugoslavia, the mentioned persons were returned to the FRY by the Yugoslav police."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this in accordance with the instructions and orders and the position of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR
utterances.text: It's in accordance with the position that all of those who were not within the regular Army of Republika Srpska could not show up as armed formations in the territory of Republika Srpska. They cannot be armed groups or formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3664, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Macar. Thank you, on behalf of the Chamber, for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We will rise all together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for your understanding regarding the length of these talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at five past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Simeon Dukic from Macedonia who is working with our team and will be joining us this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, there is a preliminary matter the parties agreed should be raised because it concerns the first witness for -- currently for next week. Mr. Nicholls has been dealing with Mr. Robinson on this matter. Their level of understanding of the details surpasses mine so I -- with the Court's permission I'd ask Mr. Nicholls to address the Court on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'll try to be brief and not take too much time. It concerns the testimony of Mr. Beara. His attorney, Mr. Ostojic, I ran into him on the balcony today and spoke with him, and he informed me that Mr. Beara indeed will testify, if called upon to do so, will not refuse, does not want to risk any type of a contempt proceedings or anything of that nature. However, he was not -- Mr. Ostojic was not aware until just very recently about Your Honours' decision relating to the Tolimir certification and he would like to -- he intends and asked me to convey to the Chamber if I could because he couldn't come into court today to convey to the Chamber that he intends next week to file a motion asking to -- for similar relief, as the Tolimir appeal. And he is requesting -- they are requesting that the summons or subpoena be stayed or postponed until a later date. I'd earlier spoken with Mr. Robinson and we had agreed, I'd thought, that if Mr. Beara was willing to testify and agreed to testify, as his attorneys had represented that he will, that he could be postponed to a later time. The final point is that my understanding is, and I just raise it, is that Mr. Ostojic is not available Monday, or is planning on flying home tomorrow and I think he's spoken to Mr. Robinson about that because he expected the testimony to be this week. I won't get into that. But for all those reasons, it seems to me to make sense not to schedule Mr. Beara for Monday morning since a motion will be coming and I just have to say practically I will be working this weekend but I would prefer not to spend all weekend working up on a cross, as Mr. Robinson as agreed before, if it's likely that it won't happen either because Mr. Beara's counsel isn't here or because the Chamber, when it's raised, is minded to lengthen the -- or stay the summons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's noted. Do we need an order from the Chamber given that he was ordered to appear on a specific day? If you could assist us, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Your order actually specified he was to appear on a date notified and we notified the date of today so I would be asking that you order that he appear on Monday so that there is a date certain and that his lawyer also appear with him on Monday. If you would like me to go into more details, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, my only submission is that's fine, but it shouldn't be Monday, doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was confused. Why on Monday? When his counsel is not available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, his counsel is here right now and understood him to be -- was supposed to be starting his testimony today, but I don't think it would be realistic that it would have been completed today anyway, so I think it would be reasonable to expect -- for him to have expected to be here on Monday in any event. But unfortunately, Mr. President, this is one of those situations where the communication with Mr. Beara's lawyer has been very difficult and one of the reasons we are in this situation is because we were never able to find out whether Mr. Beara would be testifying, would be meeting with us, what he wanted to do. He didn't file any appeal or any leave to appeal your subpoena decision so I question whether he has the right to now appeal the decision as General Tolimir did. It's been my experience that the best way to deal with this is to have the parties before you so that all of these issues can be determined sooner rather than later. And I'm concerned that if we postpone this we will start -- and you do allow an appeal, we will further delay the entire briefing schedule, et cetera, and I think we are already close to a situation where I'm not sure the Appeals Chamber will decide on appeals before we are ready to close our case and may result in some delay. So with all of those factors, with our experience with this counsel and uncertainties over what exactly Mr. Beara is going to do and the difficulties that further delay may cause, I think it's best to have him here on Monday and resolve the issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, availability of counsel is an aspect we cannot ignore in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct but this -- if the counsel is here and so I don't see any reason why he wouldn't be available on Monday if you ordered him to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to respond, if I may briefly, Your Honours. I'm not representing Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Beara, but from what I remember, Mr. Beara was scheduled to testify this morning, that is what his counsel expected, his counsel was here this morning, Mr. Robinson said we are going to delay this witness to next Monday because of scheduling difficulties, et cetera. If his overriding goal and he thought it was so important was to have everybody in the courtroom before your Chamber, he could have done that this morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, the Chamber will not hear the testimony of Mr. Beara. His testimony will be postponed to a date on which the parties could agree upon, and if the parties could agree upon the date, please bring the matter back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the parties "cannot" agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. Shall we bring in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Seselj, although I believe you must be well aware of this, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, you must know well that nobody can force me to do anything, but I state that there is no matter that can incriminate me and I'm willing to answer any questions asked by Mr. Karadzic or the opposing side that calls itself the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. I also kindly ask you to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D09105 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, do you see that statement of yours on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I read and signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page for him to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I said much more to the Defence team but this is a resume of sorts of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly the same. My answer could be a bit more lengthy but the essence certainly would not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are four associated exhibits. They are not on our 65 ter list because we hadn't interviewed Dr. Seselj at the time that list was submitted so we would ask permission that they be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the -- as regards one of the associated exhibits, that is 65 ter 13259, which is referred to in para 10, the Chamber is of the view that it does not constitute an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement in that the statement can be understood without it, so we will not admit it. But we will admit the statement as well as three other associates exhibits. Shall we assign the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter statement 1D9105 will be Exhibit D3665; 65 ter number 01221 will be Exhibit D3666; 65 ter number 13472 will be Exhibit D3667; and 65 ter number 115676 will be Exhibit D3668.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary of Dr. Seselj's statement in English. [In English] Dr. Vojislav Seselj is a native of Sarajevo. He has been active in politics since his youth. He was a leader of youth organisations during the communist regime. In February 1991, Dr. Seselj was among the founders of the Serb Radical Party and has served as its president ever since. From March 1998 until the end of 2000, Dr. Seselj was deputy prime minister of the government of the Republic of Serbia. He served continuously in the Serbian and federal parliaments from 1991 until he came to The Hague in 2003. For the past ten years, he has been defending himself at this Tribunal and is still waiting for his judgement. The Serb Radical Party advocated a multi-party democratic system, full observance of all civil rights and complete respect for the rights of national minorities. Their membership included a large number of representatives from other ethnicities. Their membership also included people of all faiths, including Muslims, Catholics, Protestants and Jews. In 1983 Dr. Seselj initiated a petition in support of the release of Alija Izetbegovic when he had been imprisoned by the communist regime. During the war in Bosnia, the Serb Radical Party never sent any volunteers to the Bosnian Krajina. He did not send anyone from the Serb Radical Party in Serbia to Bijeljina. Some local residents who were members of the Serb Radical Party fought there but Dr. Seselj is not aware of any crimes they committed. About 100 volunteers of the Serb Radical Party took part in the conflict in Zvornik as members of JNA units, while the JNA was operating there. Once the conflict was brought to an end, the JNA withdrew and the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party also withdrew. They were in Zvornik for about 15 days. These volunteers never engaged in guarding prisoners of war, nor in mistreating civilians. Dr. Seselj visited the Sarajevo area on a number of occasions during the war to provide moral support to those who were fighting there. He met Vasilije Vidovic known also as Vaske. Vaske's unit was in Cekrcici, a village outside Ilijas. During the entire war, Vaske's unit prevented Muslim forces from advancing from Visoko towards Ilijas and Sarajevo. No volunteers were sent from Belgrade to Vaske's unit, nor did Vaske ever ask for it. Dr. Seselj did not meet Vaske until 1994 and is not aware of any evidence that he or his men committed any war crimes. Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne, was a member of the Serb Radical Party from Bosnia who first volunteered to fight in Slavonia. When the war in Bosnia broke out he went to the area of Sarajevo because he was a native of that area. He first fought as part of the JNA, then joined the Ilidza brigade of the VRS and took part in the fighting for Igman Mount where he relied on a number of volunteers -- rallied a number of volunteers. Dr. Seselj received complaints from the Ilidza brigade commander and the president of Ilidza municipality that Brne was undisciplined, and he spoke to him about that in 1994 and again in 1995, asking him to be more disciplined. However, to the knowledge of Dr. Seselj, Branislav Gavrilovic did not commit any war crimes against Muslim or Croat civilians. Slavo Aleksic is a native of Herzegovina who joined the Serbian Radical Party in Grbavica. As soon as the war started he joined the VRS. The Serb Radical Party did not send volunteers to the unit of Slavko Aleksic. Dr. Seselj is not aware of any war crimes committed by Slavko Aleksic. Dr. Seselj met with Radovan Karadzic a few times each year during the war. Radovan Karadzic was a political alley of Zoran Djindjic and Vojislav Kostunica. Dr. Seselj supported Radovan Karadzic in some issues and opposed him on others such as the agreement that Karadzic made with Mate Boban in 1993. Dr. Seselj states that Radovan Karadzic did not have an antagonistic attitude towards Muslims or Croats. The allegation that he and Dr. Karadzic participated in a joint criminal enterprise to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats inhabitants from the Serbian territory is false. Dr. Karadzic never favoured the expulsion of the Muslims and Croats. Dr. Seselj was frequently in conflict -- in conflict with the other alleged members of this so-called joint criminal enterprise such as Slobodan Milosevic, who had him arrested several times, and Zeljko Raznatovic, aka Arkan, who he frequently denounced. And that is the summary of the statement of Dr. Seselj. At that moment I do not have any question for Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, you say in your statement that you were expelled from the Communist Party, I think in 1981. Am I right about the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was expelled in December 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Was membership of the Communist Party automatic from birth or was it a party that you had to make a conscious decision to join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not automatic, but the basic social status depended on that. I wouldn't have been able to become assistant lecturer or university teacher if I hadn't been a party member, at least not in a faculty of social sciences. But I joined that party of my own free will because at that time I was inclined toward a Marxist world view. I gradually liberated myself from that world view by reading theoretic literature criticising Marxism, and later I became more and more critical towards the Yugoslav communist system and the Yugoslav communist dictator, Josip Broz Tito.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as you have noted your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written witness statement. And now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Seselj. We have a limited amount of time left in the day. I'd like to commence with that portion of your statement that addresses at least to some extent your relationship with Dr. Karadzic, your connection was him. And in that regard I'd like to ask the Registrar to call up on e-court 65 ter 25195. That's an interview that was published on 24th of May, 1991, in On [phoen] and has been taken from your book, "Politics as a Conscientious Challenge." And if we could turn, please, to page 1 of the English and B/C/S page 58 of the book. Now, in the portion in English, Dr. Seselj, we see your response to a question. To put it in context, that is about while waiting for the local television show, "The Art of Living," you were staying in Pale with Radovan Karadzic, "What kind of news do you bring from Bosnia," and you state there, in part: "The Serbian Radical Party supports the policies of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Karadzic is the true leader of the Serbian people there, and enjoys undivided trust." And you indicate further you took part in the creating of a Chetnik command in mount Romanija and had a consultative meeting with Chetnik commanders from eastern Herzegovina and the Bosnian Krajina. So did that interview and your comments there accurately reflect at the time your view of Dr. Karadzic and your support for his politics and policies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, in essence, yes. In 1990, when the first parliamentary elections in the then Bosnia-Herzegovina were held, we didn't want to run at these elections because we considered that the entire Serbian people should concentrate around the Serbian Democratic Party, so we wanted to avoid a situation in which the Serbian votes would be split. Other parties did not behave that way. The Serbian Renewal Movement, the SPO, ran in some constituencies, Sipa [phoen], Nevesinje, and some others, and that's how the Serbian votes were split. The Serbs would have had at least one or two more seats in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina if that hadn't happened. We believe our political position was correct. As for the other statements, they were given at least one year before the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is about political statements and the events that happened. I had a meeting at Romanija attended by members of our party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement from Romanija, Bijeljina, Herzegovina, from Bosnian Krajina, there was Nikodin Cavic, a lawyer, who was president of our board for the -- chairman of our board for the Banja Luka region and he was sending volunteers of our party to the western Slavonian front in 1991. So perhaps you could tell me when this interview was given. There must be a date at the end of the interview, a date when it was published and the newspapers because I don't have them in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thought I indicated that initially as May 4th, 1991, the date of publication. Sorry 20 -- excuse me, 24 May 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. In -- I wanted to follow up on a couple of nuances related to the support of the SRS for the SDS, but in the interests of time it might be more useful to stick with a document that's on screen even if it bears on other topics. So if I can do that, I'd like to, in connection with another matter raised in your statement, and that is paragraphs 16 and 26, in which you address to some extent your position regarding national minorities. I wanted to turn next to page 3 of the English in this document and page 59 of the -- of your book in B/C/S. And there we see the following, the question is asked: "Has it already come to it, as you had stated in yesterday's press conference if executions of bare-handed Serbs," which by I take to mean unarmed Serbs, "begin taking place, the only remaining option is an eye-for-an-eye action." And the response you provide is: "Yes, it has. We have already deployed several Chetnik groups in Zagreb and other towns across Croatia which are trained in sabotage and other terrorist activities. If Serbian civilians start to be massacred the Chetniks will strike at Zagreb and other concentrations of Croats using their full strength. You know when one retaliates revenge is blind. There would be innocent victims but what can you do? Let the Croats think about that first. We shall not strike first but if they should strike, we are not even going to bother where our blows land. Also, unless the army disarms the Ustashas immediately there will be a lot of blood." And did that correctly reflect your position in May of 1991, regarding the actions that you intended for the Chetnik groups to take in response to any attacks on Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: This position, not only reflects my opinion from 1991, but also my opinion of today. I even today think that somebody threatens the Serbian people anywhere, the Serbs should reply in kind. There must be -- there must come an end of the destruction of the Serbian people and the devastation of Serbian towns and villages. But this was a bluff about the existence of Chetnik groups in Zagreb. We didn't have such groups. But I deliberately uttered such a threat publicly in order to relieve the Croatian pressure on the Serbs because that was a time when tens of thousands of Serbs were leaving Croatian towns because of Tudjman's regime, partly villages too but mostly towns. That was in May 1991. The Serbs were fleeing Zagreb, Varazdin, Sisak and many other towns in masses. They were being tortured, many Serbian civilians were killed, many were tortured, many were robbed and so on. And this is a threat, whether or not it had effect, I unfortunately didn't have enough power to implement that threat, and that was a time when the JNA still was not involved in the conflict. It was a time when the Serbs were resisting, when there was a greater concentration of them, whichever way they could. It was mostly in villages. In towns they couldn't. They were preventing the Croatian police from entering their places and they were defending themselves. That's when the Serbian Radical Party sent many volunteers to the Slavonian villages and they were helping in that defence. That was a time when we -- when our policy was that of active defence because the JNA was standing apart. They were neutral force which only intervened from time to time to stop a conflict, mostly when the Croats were hit by hard blows and then they would help them to get out of their encirclement and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have time for one more excerpt from that publication and that's found at page 6 of the English and page 61 through 62 of the book in B/C/S. And here, the discussion moves on to the issue of Bosnia. And there, we see the following excerpt. Question is asked: "But what about Bosnia, let alone the others?" Your response is: "Bosnia is undoubtedly Serbian and if any Muslim fundamentalists do not like that, they will have to pack their suitcases and leave." The interviewer asks: "But the majority of its population is Muslim." Your response is: "So what? If they become loyal citizens of Serbia, they will enjoy full citizens' rights and human freedoms. If not, they will have to start packing." The interviewer asks: "Is Europe going to observe it calmly?" And your response is: "How could Europe prevent it? Would Europe be willing to go to war to prevent it? I do not think so." And was that an accurate reflection of your position regarding Bosnia, essentially who was entitled or which group was entitled to authority over its territory and what would be in your view an appropriate response by those Muslims who objected to Serbian control of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: As regards my threats to the Islamic fundamentalists, they are still valid. Consider them still valid anywhere. Even ten years before the war, I stood out as a fighter against Islamic fundamentalism because it was gaining strength mostly in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as regards Bosnia-Herzegovina and its ethnic composition, it is always been exclusively inhabited by Serbs, over 90 per cent of Serbs. There may be a Czech here and there or a pole, maybe a Hungarian or Ukrainian who settled there at Austro-Hungarian times, but over 90 per cent of the inhabitants are Serbs: Orthodox Serbs, Muslim Serbs and Catholic Serbs. And the policy of my party is a policy of the universal Serb ethnic unity. I made an appeal to the Serbs of Muslim faith which was issued in July 1990, and it was sent to the population of Sarajevo and some other places as early as March. You can check that in documents. I set out an appeal, an open letter to them, warning them of the threats arising from the political situation and appealing to them to avoid the tragic events from the Second World War when they were instrumentalised by the Croats. Of course, not all Muslims. It was my goal, therefore, to preserve the Serbian ethnic being, the -- because the Orthodox Serbs, Catholic Serbs and Muslim Serbs are one people. The Hague Tribunal insisted on the existence of a Bosnian language, but these are vain efforts. There is no such thing as the Bosnian language. The Croats thought up their own language 150 years ago. The original Croatian language was Cakavian, and then they accepted a slow Slovenian variant, a Slovenian dialect, Kajkavian -- am I speaking too fast? I'll finish fast, but it's important for me to explain so that you may know, sir. And up until 1850, the Croats didn't have their standard language. Then they adopted the Serbian language as their standard language, so that in that way, they could assimilate a large group of Catholic Serbs because the Croatian nation is an artificial nation under the direct patronage of the Catholic church. I wrote a book that comprises 1.000 pages and which aroused much attention in scientific circles all over the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you have answered the question. We will adjourn for today and the week, and resume on Monday morning at 9.00. Hearing is adjourned.
